title: Whale Spend Report
scenario: Jonas Lindgren, a live-operations analyst at a Helsinki mobile game studio, prepares a weekly report on spending. It shows that two percent of players generate seventy percent of revenue, and some of those top spenders show signs of compulsion: purchases at three in the morning, repeated refund requests, and messages apologising to family. The studio's director asks him to build a tool that identifies these players so the team can send them personalised offers. Jonas could instead propose using the same identification to cap spending. The next sprint planning is tomorrow morning.
options: Build the identification tool for targeted offers, since players are adults making free choices and revenue sustains the studio's staff and free players.
Build it to trigger spending limits and cooling-off prompts for at-risk players, accepting a revenue drop and conflict with the director.
Build the neutral tool and let leadership decide how to use it, documenting the risk that the data shows compulsion.

title: A Teenager's Card in the Cupboard
scenario: Dolores Villanueva, a Madrid mother, discovers that her fourteen-year-old son Mateo has spent eleven hundred euros on a football game's card packs using her stored card details. Mateo is ashamed and has been skipping meals at school to hide the evidence. The publisher's policy refunds only for fraud, not for minors' purchases, though a consumer group says refunds can be won by complaint. Dolores could file a chargeback claiming unauthorised payment, which is not entirely true, or contact the company honestly and probably lose the money. Her bank closes disputes in two days.
options: File the chargeback as an unauthorised transaction, since the company designed the system to exploit children and a refund is only fair.
Explain honestly to the company and the bank that her son made the purchases, accepting the loss and teaching him accountability.
Complain through the consumer authority citing misleading design aimed at minors, accepting a slower, uncertain route without misstating facts.

title: Loot Box Odds Disclosure
scenario: Aisha Khan is a compliance lawyer for a Karachi-founded game developer selling globally. A new regulation in one market requires publishing exact drop rates for randomized rewards, and the rates for the rarest items are very low. Revealing them would likely reduce sales sharply in that market. She could comply fully, comply in a way that is technically accurate but buried several menus deep, or geo-block the market. Her CEO asks for her recommendation, noting the regulator is small and enforcement uncertain, and the launch is in ten days.
options: Comply technically by burying the odds in menus, meeting the letter of the law while limiting the damage to sales.
Display the exact odds prominently at the point of purchase, accepting lower revenue in that market.
Geo-block that market altogether, avoiding both the compliance cost and any question of deceiving players there.
tension: letter vs. spirit of the law

title: The Lottery Kiosk Regular
scenario: Hemant Kulkarni runs a corner shop in Pune that sells lottery tickets, which bring commission and foot traffic. A regular, an auto-rickshaw driver named Santosh, spends roughly half his daily earnings on tickets and has begun borrowing from other customers. Hemant has also seen his wife leave the shop in tears. The licence does not oblige him to turn anyone away, and refusing Santosh might drive him to a rougher gambling den. Hemant's margins on tickets pay the shop's rent. Santosh walks in every evening at six.
options: Keep selling to Santosh as usual, since adults decide how to spend their money and the licence permits it.
Refuse to sell to Santosh and tell him why, accepting the loss of income and the chance that he gambles elsewhere.
Limit the number of tickets sold to him each day, speak to him kindly, and offer him information about a counseling service.

title: Casino Host's Quiet Phone Call
scenario: Valentina Rossi, a VIP host at a Macau casino, has built a friendly relationship with Mr. Chan, a property developer who loses heavily on weekends. This week he lost three million dollars, borrowed from the casino's credit line, and told her he is hiding the losses from his business partners. The casino pays her bonuses based on her clients' play, and Mr. Chan is arriving tonight. She could arrange his usual suite and credit, quietly suggest a break, or notify the casino's responsible gambling team, which would likely ban him.
options: Welcome him as usual and extend credit within his limits, since he is an experienced adult and the casino's relationship is built on trust.
Speak to him privately and suggest he skip this weekend, without involving anyone else, relying on friendship rather than rules.
Refer him to the responsible gambling team, accepting the end of the relationship and the loss to her bonus.

title: Streamer's Gambling Sponsorship
scenario: Kasper Nowak, a popular Polish streamer with many teenage viewers, is offered a lucrative sponsorship by an online casino operating through a licensing loophole. The contract requires him to play on camera and share a promo code, with winnings shown but losses not. His channel's income has declined, and the deal would cover two years of rent and equipment. Previous sponsors included energy drinks and skincare brands. His moderator says chat contains minors and warns that gambling advertising to them is harmful. A response is due tomorrow.
options: Accept the sponsorship with age warnings, since the product is legal for adults and he cannot control who watches.
Decline the sponsorship entirely, accepting financial strain to avoid exposing minors to gambling content.
Accept but negotiate to show losses as well as wins and to apply age-gating on stream, risking the sponsor's withdrawal.
tension: income vs. responsibility to young audiences

title: Daily Login Streak Redesign
scenario: Ayumi Sato, a game designer in Fukuoka, is responsible for a children's puzzle game that earns steady money through a daily streak system: miss a day and you lose your progress, unless you buy a streak restore. Analytics show children as young as eight panicking when they miss a day. Parents have posted frustrated reviews. Removing the penalty would reduce streak-restore revenue by roughly a fifth, and the producer says the studio's next project depends on the income. Ayumi has authority over the retention design and the redesign must be locked by Friday.
options: Keep the streak penalty as it is, since it keeps players engaged and funds future projects the studio hopes to make.
Remove the loss penalty and restore feature, making streaks purely rewarding and accepting the revenue drop.
Keep the streak but offer one free automatic restore per week, softening the pressure while retaining some revenue.

title: Bookmaker's Self-Exclusion Request
scenario: Customer service agent Obinna Eze at a betting company in Lagos receives a tearful call from a customer, Chiamaka, begging to be permanently blocked after losing her savings. The company's policy requires verifying identity and allows a seven-day cooling-off, not a permanent ban without extra paperwork. She says she cannot wait a week and fears placing another bet tonight. Obinna has an admin tool that could block her immediately but it is restricted to supervisors. His supervisor is unreachable until morning. The system will log his action under his name.
options: Follow policy and offer the seven-day cooling-off, since unauthorised use of the admin tool breaks rules he's expected to follow.
Use the admin tool to block her immediately, accepting the risk of disciplinary action to protect her tonight.
Tell her to remove her payment cards and set bank limits herself while he escalates the case urgently to his supervisor.
tension: personal risk vs. duty of care

title: Raffle for the Hospice
scenario: Brigid O'Donnell organises fundraisers for a hospice in County Clare. A successful annual raffle sells tickets of fifty euros each, with a car as top prize, and raises a third of the hospice's budget. This year a volunteer notes that elderly local people on tight incomes are buying many tickets, hoping to win and believing it helps the hospice that cared for relatives. A board member suggests introducing a cap on tickets per buyer, which would reduce income. Printing deadlines for the tickets are in two days, and Brigid has the deciding voice.
options: Run the raffle as in past years, since people give freely and the hospice's funding depends on it.
Introduce a per-buyer ticket cap and alternative ways to give, accepting lower funds to avoid encouraging overspending.
Keep the raffle uncapped but add clear messages that donations are welcome without tickets and that odds are poor.
tension: autonomy vs. protection of the vulnerable

title: Fantasy Sports for Students
scenario: Rhys Pritchard, a marketing manager at a Cardiff fantasy-sports startup, drafts a campaign targeting university freshmen with free-entry contests that move to paid leagues once they have friends in the system. Campus data suggests signups will be huge. The product is legal for those over eighteen, and the company's terms include responsible-play tools. A university counsellor has emailed that students already struggle with gambling debts. Rhys's director wants the campaign materials approved by the end of the week, and the launch aligns with orientation week.
options: Launch the campaign as designed on campuses, since the audience is legally adult and the product includes safeguards.
Move the campaign away from universities toward general adult audiences, losing the strongest growth channel.
Run the campus campaign but without the free-to-paid conversion mechanics and with prominent spending limit tools.
tension: growth vs. vulnerability of young adults

title: The Spin Wheel and the Pensioner Grandmother
scenario: Oksana Melnyk works as a UX researcher at a Kyiv company that makes a free-to-play slot app popular with older adults. In interviews, she meets Halyna, seventy-six, who plays for hours alone and spends a modest but growing sum of her pension. Halyna says the game keeps her company after her husband's death. The design includes near-miss animations and flashing rewards that Oksana's testing shows prolong sessions. She is to present her findings to the product team on Monday and must decide how much of what she learned to include.
options: Present the engagement findings as asked, without drawing attention to the vulnerability of older players, to keep her relationship with the team.
Present the vulnerability findings in full and recommend removing near-miss animations, accepting that the team may resent her.
Present all findings neutrally and ask the team to decide on safeguards, sharing the facts without recommending a specific change.

title: A Teacher and the Classroom Betting Pool
scenario: Mr. Karim Bensaid teaches mathematics at a Casablanca secondary school, where he finds that several boys run a betting pool on football matches, collecting small stakes from classmates. A younger student, Anas, has lost his bus money for a month. Karim could report this to the headmaster, who would likely suspend the organisers, or use the situation in a lesson on probability. The organisers are clever students from poor homes, and one is his best mathematics pupil. Parents are unaware. Karim must act before the weekend's big match.
options: Report the betting pool to the headmaster, as school rules require, and accept the punishment that follows for the organisers.
Address it in a probability lesson and talk privately with the organisers, trying to end the pool without formal discipline.
Speak with Anas's parents and the organisers separately, arranging repayment of stakes while avoiding school-level punishment.

title: Personalised Offers After a Bad Week
scenario: Cecilia Moreno, a data engineer at a Mexico City sports-betting app, is asked to deploy a model that predicts when a user has had a losing streak and then sends a bonus offer to keep them playing. Early tests show it increases retention by thirty percent. Her colleague points out that the same signal could be used to trigger a gentle check-in message. Cecilia's team lead says responsible-gaming features are handled by another department. The deployment window is next Tuesday, and she is the only engineer who understands the model fully.
options: Deploy the retention model as specified, since responsible-gaming duties belong to another department and her job is to build.
Refuse to deploy it until the loss-streak signal is used for check-ins rather than offers, accepting friction with her lead.
Deploy it but exclude users who show markers of heavy losses, a compromise that reduces the effect but retains the model.
tension: division of responsibility vs. moral agency

title: Auction House for Pets
scenario: Teuila Tuilagi runs an online collectibles marketplace in Auckland where users buy mystery boxes containing trading cards of random value. Sales soar among teenagers who buy repeatedly, hoping for rare cards. Some boxes contain items worth far less than the price. An independent collectors' forum accuses the marketplace of acting like a gambling operation without a licence. Teuila could add odds disclosure and age verification at some cost, accept the legal grey area, or retire mystery boxes entirely. Investors meet on Friday and ask what she plans.
options: Keep mystery boxes as they are, since they are a popular, legal retail format and the forum's accusation is not a legal finding.
Add odds disclosure and age verification, accepting reduced sales and delays in launching new box lines.
Retire mystery boxes and sell known items directly, giving up a major revenue stream to avoid the gambling resemblance.

title: Coins for the Village Raffle App
scenario: Samir Haddad, who teaches coding in a Jordanian youth centre, helps students build a mobile app for a village football club's fundraising raffle. Local elders love it, and sales have tripled. A student, Rana, notices that the same few households are buying the most tickets and that the odds are not published. The app has no age check, and some children use their parents' phones. Samir could add transparency features, which would take the students' remaining term, or leave the app as is since the raffle benefits the club's youth programs.
options: Leave the app as is and focus on finishing it, since the elders support it and the benefits go to the local youth club.
Add odds publication, ticket limits and age checks, using the remaining term and delaying the fundraising.
Pause the app and discuss with the club committee whether to continue raffles at all, letting the community decide.
tension: community benefit vs. harm to vulnerable households

title: Dopamine Dashboard in the Language App
scenario: Nikolai Petrov is a growth lead at a Sofia-based language-learning startup. Experiments show that adding slot-machine style reward chests increases daily use by thirty-five percent, though learning outcomes are flat. Users report feeling anxious without their streak. Investors pressure growth numbers ahead of a funding round next month. Nikolai believes language learning is a worthy goal but sees little evidence that rewards help it. The product council meets in two days and he must either champion the feature or oppose it.
options: Champion the reward chests, since engagement is a precondition of learning and the funding round will let the company improve its teaching.
Oppose the feature on grounds of manipulative design and propose alternative engagement methods tied to actual learning progress.
Support a limited rollout to half of users with an honest test of learning outcomes, delaying the funding story but gathering evidence.

title: Spouse's Lottery Syndicate Money
scenario: Chinedu Eze-Brandt, a Hamburg bank branch manager, notices that a customer, Frau Weiss, regularly transfers large sums to an overseas 'lottery syndicate' with promises of imminent winnings. The transfers resemble advance-fee fraud, but the customer insists the syndicate is genuine, and her husband has recently died. Bank policy lets staff delay suspicious transfers briefly, but not block them. She is at the counter requesting another transfer of five thousand euros. Customer data protection rules limit what Chinedu can discuss with her family or others.
options: Process the transfer after a clear verbal warning, respecting her right to decide even if the decision looks unwise.
Delay the transfer as far as policy allows and refer her case to the fraud team, even if it upsets her.
Speak with her at length in private and ask permission to contact her sister, trying to persuade rather than override.
tension: customer autonomy vs. protection from fraud

title: Esports Betting Sponsor for a Student Team
scenario: Coach Gabriela Alves leads a Brazilian university esports team that is offered fifteen thousand reais by a betting company for its jerseys and streams. The team's travel to a national tournament depends on this money, and the university has no budget for it. Several players are under nineteen. Previous teams in the league have accepted similar deals without public criticism. The student union president argues that associating with betting at a university sends the wrong message. Gabriela must tell the sponsor yes or no by Thursday.
options: Accept the sponsorship, since the team needs the funds and the sponsor's product is legal in the country.
Decline and fundraise through smaller means, risking the team's attendance at the national tournament.
Accept but restrict logos from appearing on streams directed at underage viewers and add a responsible-gaming message.

title: Free Spins for a Recovering Gambler
scenario: Stellan Berg, a CRM manager at an online casino in Malta, is reviewing an automated email sent to lapsed customers offering fifty free spins. He sees that the list includes Mr. Evans, who self-excluded eleven months ago and has not yet reached the cooling-off period required for reinstatement. A flaw in the exclusion database let him slip through. Fixing the database would take weeks, while pulling the whole campaign would anger the marketing director and cost thousands of euros. The email is scheduled to send at noon today.
options: Remove Mr. Evans manually and let the campaign proceed, then log the database issue for later repair.
Halt the entire campaign until the database flaw is fixed, protecting all self-excluded customers who might be on the list.
Send the campaign as scheduled and report the flaw afterwards, as the cost and delay of stopping seems disproportionate.
tension: protection of excluded customers vs. business cost

title: Betting Debt and the Family Farm
scenario: Pita Ravuvu, an elder in a Fijian village, learns that his nephew Joeli has lost money on online poker, borrowed from a lender, and put his share of communal land lease income forward as security. The land is owned jointly by the clan and the lease income is shared. The lender has threatened to sue. The clan could pay the debt to protect the lease, shaming Joeli and drawing on communal funds. Or they could refuse and let the case go to court, possibly threatening the family's lease arrangements. Pita must advise the council this evening.
options: Advise the clan to pay the debt from communal funds to protect the lease, with Joeli repaying through labour over time.
Advise refusing to pay and letting Joeli face the consequences alone, protecting communal resources and sending a firm message.
Advise paying only after Joeli commits to counselling and surrenders his income share until the debt is cleared.

title: Shared Account and the Lottery Syndicate Cheat
scenario: Ingrid Haugen leads a workplace lottery syndicate of twelve colleagues at a Bergen shipping firm. The group's account shows a win of four hundred thousand kroner, but Ingrid discovers that one member, Ole, had paid his share late and arguably missed the draw cutoff. The rules are informal. Ole is in financial trouble, and his late payment was due to a delay in his salary. Splitting twelve ways would be the generous reading, but eleven others could claim a larger share. Ingrid holds the money and has to announce the split on Friday.
options: Split among all twelve equally, giving Ole his share, since the rules were informal and he intended to participate.
Split among the eleven who paid on time, applying the cutoff rule as everyone understood it in principle.
Split equally but let the group vote openly on whether Ole's late payment should reduce his share.

title: Wellness App Pays You to Lose
scenario: Divya Menon is head of product at a Bengaluru fitness and weight-loss app that wants to introduce a wagering feature: users stake their own money on meeting goals and lose it if they fail, the pooled losses going to those who succeed. Behavioral studies suggest this works strongly for motivation. But critics note it resembles gambling, and those with eating disorders could be harmed. Regulators have not addressed it. Divya's team estimates it could double revenue. The product roadmap must be signed off by her at the end of the week.
options: Launch the wagering feature, since it helps users meet goals they set themselves and the stakes are voluntary.
Cancel the feature because the risk to vulnerable users with eating disorders and the gambling resemblance are too serious.
Launch it with caps on stakes, exclusion of users with certain health indicators, and mandatory cooling-off periods.
tension: behavioral benefit vs. risk of harm

title: Pawnshop and the Wedding Ring
scenario: Nomvula Zulu operates a pawnshop in Durban. A young man, Thulani, pawns his late mother's ring for gambling money at a nearby casino, and she recognises him as a regular who always redeems nothing. The ring's sentimental value is clear. The law lets her take pawns without questioning purpose, and refusing would send him to another pawnbroker. She could offer him a fair price, a lower price to discourage him, or refuse, perhaps advising him to go home. A queue is forming behind him.
options: Accept the pawn at a fair price, since it is a lawful transaction and the decision belongs to him.
Refuse the pawn and gently suggest he reconsider, accepting the loss of business and the chance he goes elsewhere.
Accept the ring but hold it for an extended period before sale and tell him how to redeem it cheaply later.

title: Child's Birthday and the Prize Wheel
scenario: Amelie Dubois, who runs a Quebec arcade, has discovered that children aged seven to ten prefer machines dispensing tickets redeemed for toys, which are essentially slot machines with a prize wheel. Parents love that the children are occupied, but a mother, Sophie, complains that her child begged for money to play after one visit. Removing the machines would cut a third of weekday revenue. Alternatives exist that reward skill rather than chance, but cost more to install. The new season's orders for machines must be confirmed on Wednesday.
options: Keep ordering the chance-based ticket machines, since children enjoy them, parents choose to bring them, and the harm is hard to prove.
Replace them with skill-based machines even at greater cost, reducing the sense of gambling for children.
Keep some chance machines but limit plays per visit and put visible price information on each machine.

title: The Shopkeeper's Scratch Cards
scenario: Adjoa Mensah, a school bursar in Kumasi, recognises that her brother-in-law, who runs a kiosk outside the school, sells scratch cards to pupils at break time. The cards cost little and each carries a small chance of a prize. Some pupils spend their lunch money. Reporting him would fracture family relations, and he depends on this income for his children's school fees. The headmaster has asked bursars to report on anything affecting pupils' welfare. Adjoa must submit her weekly report tomorrow morning.
options: Include the kiosk in her report, as her role requires, and accept the strain on her family.
Speak to her brother-in-law first and ask him to stop selling to pupils in uniform, leaving the report silent if he agrees.
Leave it out of the report altogether, protecting family ties and trusting that the sums involved are small.
